st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between average assisted performance and the distribution of gains, while materially extending it by identifying AI Interaction Competence—especially elicitation, filtering and verification—as a predictor of who benefits. It also provides experimental evidence that conceptual scaffolding can reduce performance inequality without lowering mean performance, though it does not establish employment, income or career effects.

Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source accepts that AI access and average task gains do not translate uniformly into productivity or capability. It materially extends the cluster by identifying AI Interaction Competence as a human-capital mechanism and reporting causal evidence that training and conceptual scaffolding can reduce performance dispersion without lowering mean performance.
qs: Conceptually, AIC is a new dimension of human capital that determines how individuals translate AI access into performance.

Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts that GenAI can produce immediate productivity gains while showing that those gains depend materially on user competence and workflow design. Its randomized experiment adds concrete evidence that novice outcomes can become more unequal, and that conceptual scaffolding can reduce this dispersion without sacrificing average performance. Although the experiment simulates early-career knowledge work rather than legal practice directly, it strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on training, verification and organisational complements.
qs: Improvements were not predicted by GPA or prior knowledge, but      by AI Interaction Competence (AIC) — the ability to elicit, filter, and verify model outputs.

Notably, a scaffolding intervention (conceptual roadmaps and sequencing) reduced this dispersion by nearly 40% without lowering the mean, demonstrating that small process changes can stabilize outcomes.

st.t: Skill gaps: Assisted equality can hide learning divides
st.an: The source supports the distinction between average AI-assisted gains and unequal underlying capabilities, then materially develops it by identifying AI Interaction Competence as a new basis of advantage. It also shows that structured scaffolding may reduce the resulting dispersion, although the intervention evidence is only weakly significant and limited to short-term student learning.

Whereas unguided LLM use amplified differences in AIC levels, the roadmap reduced these disparities by providing a structured path through the material.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that task-level gains depend on human expertise, verification and workflow design, then materially extends it with randomized evidence that AI Interaction Competence drives heterogeneous gains and that lightweight scaffolding can reduce performance dispersion. Its applicability to legal work remains indirect because the experiment used university students in a simulated knowledge-work setting.
qs: Together, these insights reframe GenAI adoption as a problem of capability design: organizations must align technology, human skill, and workflow structure to capture value consistently.

Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.

st.t: AI learning: Interaction skill shapes novice gains
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s qualified proposition: randomized LLM access improved short-term exam scores, but the evidence does not establish broad or persistent novice equalization. It also finds that competence, preferences, scaffolding and differential attrition condition the observed benefits.
qs: The average post-intervention exam score among LLM participants was M = .56, SD = .26, compared to M = .48, SD = .23 in the baseline group.

These mismatches complicate the integration of GenAI into knowledge-work training: they suggest that access alone will not guarantee equity, since participants’ decisions about how to learn do not always align with where they learn best.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports evaluating practical AI effects through randomized human-performance comparisons rather than inferring productivity from access or adoption. It also separates measured learning and application from engagement, preferences and perceived capability, while testing heterogeneity across workers and implementation choices. Because the supplied excerpts report design rather than treatment outcomes, it does not establish whether AI ultimately saves time, improves learning or narrows capability gaps.
qs: We randomize access to:     (*) A GenAI condition (LLM-assisted self-study and problem solving), and     (*) A baseline condition (traditional resources such as manuals, articles, recorded trainings, and peer discussions; no LLM access).
Beyond performance scores, we also assess engagement, dropout patterns, and resource preferences to capture knowledge workers’ revealed judgments about the relative value of LLMs.

kp.k: Student experiment models early-career knowledge work
kp.d: This 2026 working paper studies technical learning rather than legal services directly. The randomized experiment involved 179 Texas A&M University participants, predominantly engineering undergraduates, with some graduate and business students. The authors treat rapidly learning and applying unfamiliar technical information as an analogue for early-career professional work; the measured outcome is exam performance, used as a productivity proxy.
qs: The intervention was conducted at Texas A&M University with a total of 179 participants.

Although the participants were university students, the task environment—rapidly acquir- ing and applying unfamiliar technical information under time constraints—closely mirrors cognitive work processes in professional domains such as consulting, analytics, engineering, and research.
The primary outcome is individual task performance (a proxy for knowledge-work productivity).

kp.k: Randomization compares ChatGPT-only learning with traditional resources
kp.d: Participants studied LLMs for a minimum of three hours daily over three consecutive days. A 15-item baseline exam classified those answering at least eight correctly as advanced and others as novices. Primary randomization assigned non-LLM resources or exclusively free ChatGPT; novice ChatGPT users received secondary randomization to standard study, four hours daily, conceptual scaffolding, or peer collaboration. The post-intervention exam contained 28 multiple-choice questions focused on LLM knowledge; participants could bring a one-page cheat sheet. Completion paid $50, with an additional $150 for the top 10%.
qs: Participants were instructed to dedicate a minimum of 3 hours per day for 3 consecutive days to self-study.
Restricted to using only the free version of ChatGPT (paid subscriptions prohib- ited).
Within the LLM condition, novice participants were further randomized into one of four scaffolding sub-conditions.
the top 10% of participants on the post-intervention exam received an extra $150.

kp.k: LLM access improved average exam performance
kp.d: The LLM condition achieved a mean normalized post-exam score of .56 (SD .26), versus .48 (SD .23) with traditional resources. The reported treatment coefficient remained positive and significant at p < 0.05 after controls for baseline score, GPA, gender, and study preferences. The discussion characterizes this as an approximate 17% productivity lift, although the directly measured outcome was technical-learning performance, not workplace output.
qs: The average post-intervention exam score among LLM participants was M = .56, SD = .26, compared to M = .48, SD = .23 in the baseline group.
The treatment coefficient remained positive and statistically significant (p < 0.05).
GenAI access translated into an approximate 17% productivity lift

kp.k: Differential dropout qualifies reported performance comparisons
kp.d: Twenty baseline participants withdrew compared with nine LLM participants, with a reported chi-square p < 0.01. All performance analyses used completers. Although baseline participants generally cited illness or scheduling conflicts, the authors interpret the imbalance as reduced motivation without LLM access and explicitly acknowledge bias favoring the LLM group. Resource preferences were 69% for LLMs, 64% for lectures, 67% for YouTube tutorials, and 40% for textbooks; the motivational explanation is the authors' interpretation rather than participants' stated reason for withdrawal.
qs: Overall, 20 participants in the baseline group withdrew before the post-intervention exam, compared to only 9 in the LLM group.
Baseline participants most commonly cited illness or scheduling conflicts
This pattern not only biased final outcomes in favor of the LLM group but also illustrates how technology availability can shape engagement itself.
All analyses use the completer sample (post-intervention exam scores available)

kp.k: AI interaction competence supplies the central complementarity mechanism
kp.d: The authors define AI Interaction Competence (AIC) as precise prompting, filtering and verifying outputs, and iterative refinement combining human judgment with model suggestions. Their framework treats GenAI as interactive augmentation: access creates value unevenly because users differ in their ability to direct, check, and apply generated material. This is a proposed dimension of human capital, distinct from conventional subject knowledge or academic credentials.
qs: AIC is defined as the set of practical skills and habits that enable an individual to use generative AI systems effectively and reliably in their work.
Filter and verify generative AI’s outputs for accuracy, bias, and relevance rather than accepting them at face value.
Iterate interactively, refining inputs and combining human judgment with machine suggestions to improve quality and efficiency.
GenAI is not merely a substitute for labor but a multiplier of competence

kp.k: AIC, not academic markers, moderated reported treatment gains
kp.d: GPA and baseline knowledge interactions with treatment were statistically insignificant (p = 0.59 and p = 0.2 respectively), whereas Treatment × AIC was positive and significant at p < 0.05. A significant three-way interaction between treatment, baseline score, and AIC indicated larger novice benefits conditional on high AIC. The authors interpret this as an emerging inequality axis; their stronger language about compressing conventional academic inequality goes beyond the narrower reported finding of nonsignificant academic-marker moderation. The abstract also states that low-AIC users experienced limited or negative marginal returns.
qs: The interaction between GPA and treatment assignment was small and statistically insignificant (p = 0.59).
pre-intervention exam scores, which measure prior topic-specific knowledge, did not significantly interact with treatment status (p = 0.2).
novice learners (i.e., those with low prior knowledge) benefited more from LLM-assisted study, but only if they had high AIC levels.
High-AIC participants realized outsized gains; low-AIC participants saw limited or even negative marginal returns.

kp.k: AIC measurement descriptions differ across sections
kp.d: The pre-intervention survey section lists self-assessed AIC knowledge, but the results state that AIC was neither self-assessed nor tested in the baseline exam and instead was inferred from behavioral performance. The results report self-assessment/performance correlations of .71 for general ML knowledge (p < .01), .6 for LLM-specific knowledge (p < .01), and .46 for AIC (p < .05), while treating the latter as a skill-measurement association rather than calibration. These differing descriptions qualify how the reported AIC moderator should be understood.
qs: Self-assessed knowledge of LLM Interaction Competence (AIC)
Importantly, AIC was not itself a domain of self-assessment but rather inferred from behavioral performance
the practical skill in prompting and filtering that participants were neither asked to self-assess nor tested on in the pre-intervention exam.

kp.k: Conceptual scaffolding preferentially helped low-AIC novices
kp.d: Novices receiving a conceptual roadmap scored .45 (SD .14), versus .38 (SD .22) among unguided LLM novices. Both the mean difference and negative scaffolding × AIC interaction were only weakly significant (.05 < p < .10). The authors interpret the lower dispersion and diminishing scaffolding benefits at higher AIC as evidence that structured sequencing helps weaker AI users most. The discussion additionally reports a roughly 47% increase in novice standard deviation under GenAI and nearly 40% reduction with scaffolding.
qs: The average post-intervention exam score among scaffolded novices was M = .45, SD = .14, compared to M = .38, SD = .22 in the baseline LLM group, with a weakly significant difference (p > .05, p < .10).
conceptual scaffolding had its greatest impact on participants with low AIC, while high-skill participants derived little additional benefit.
dispersion among novices increased by roughly 47% in standard deviation—more than doubling the variance.
a scaffolding intervention (conceptual roadmaps and sequencing) reduced this dispersion by nearly 40% without lowering the mean

kp.k: Additional required study time did not improve performance
kp.d: Increasing novice study requirements from three to four hours per day produced a mean score of .37 (SD .22), statistically indistinguishable from unguided LLM novices at .38 (SD .23) in this comparison. Controlled OLS models found no significant additional-time effect. The authors interpret this as diminishing returns to exposure without effective strategies, noting some reported frustration. Although peer collaboration was an experimental arm, the results discussion does not report its treatment effect.
qs: extending the daily study requirement from three to four hours produced no significant performance gains.
Novices in the “more time” group scored M = .37, SD = .22, statistically indistinguishable from unguided LLM novices, M = .38, SD = .23.
Without scaffolding or high AIC levels, more time-on-task produced diminishing returns, and in some cases, participants reported frustration with the extended requirement.

kp.k: Preference for AI is an imperfect competence signal
kp.d: LLM-preferring participants had higher AIC on average (Mann–Whitney p < .05), but the preference–competence correlation was only r = 0.26. The authors distinguish enthusiastic low-skill users from skilled users preferring other resources. They speculate that the latter value social learning; the reported logistic association did not reach conventional significance (p ≈ 0.1). They explicitly leave the motivations of enthusiastic low-skill users unresolved.
qs: the correlation between preference and ability was only small to moderate (r = 0.26)
it is unclear whether their preference reflects optimism, overconfidence, or a lack of awareness of their limitations.
their reluctance to rely on LLMs may stem not from inability but from a desire for the social and collaborative dimensions of learning
it did not reach conventional levels of significance (p ≈ 0.1).

kp.k: Expandable learning creates possible navigational burdens
kp.d: Exploratory analysis suggested that learning gains declined more strongly with initial knowledge in the non-LLM condition than in standard LLM study, despite a nonsignificant formal treatment–baseline-score interaction. The authors hypothesize that tailored explanations, follow-up questions, examples, and redirection make LLM learning less bounded by fixed materials. They also suggest that very low-knowledge learners may lack sufficient grounding to navigate this flexibility, recognize misleading explanations, and consolidate understanding. These are proposed mechanisms, not established treatment findings.
qs: Although the formal interaction between treatment and pre-intervention exam score is not statistically significant in our main specification

Participants can request tailored explanations, ask follow-up questions, compare concepts, generate examples, test partial understanding, and continuously redirect the material toward their own confusions.
A plausible mechanism is that open-ended LLM use creates navigational demands of its own.

kp.k: Authors recommend capability development rather than procurement alone
kp.d: The managerial recommendation is to diagnose AIC gaps, train prompting, verification, and synthesis, and embed prompt templates, review checklists, and feedback in onboarding and workflows. The discussion asserts that 60–90-minute interventions can raise the performance floor and that such process interventions reduce variance by about one-third without reducing the mean. These training claims should be distinguished from the described randomized interventions, which test roadmaps, additional time, and peer collaboration rather than a separately reported 60–90-minute micro-training arm. Application to professional knowledge work is the authors' cross-domain extension.
qs: These insights reframe AI adoption as a problem of capability design rather than tool procurement.
Firms can address this gap through targeted micro-training that focuses on prompting logic, verification heuristics, and synthesis structure.
Short interventions of 60–90 minutes can meaningfully raise the performance floor, especially when coupled with light scaffolds such as standardized prompt templates or review checklists.
reduce performance variance by about one-third without diminishing the mean.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Anand and Idan claim that GenAI improves average learning performance but distributes gains unevenly according to AI Interaction Competence (AIC); structured guidance can make those gains more consistent.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about education and knowledge work, not a study of legal services. The authors report higher post-study performance with LLM access and characterize the difference as an approximately 17% productivity lift. They argue that prompting, filtering, verification, and application skills—not GPA or prior subject knowledge—moderate the benefits. High-AIC novices benefit especially strongly, while low-AIC users obtain smaller gains; the abstract also claims limited or negative marginal returns for low-AIC participants. The authors interpret this as a new axis of capability inequality. Conceptual roadmaps reportedly improve novice outcomes and reduce dispersion, particularly for low-AIC users, whereas increasing required study time does not significantly improve performance. They also claim that LLM availability supports engagement, while preferences for LLMs are imperfect indicators of competence. Their managerial prediction is that firms combining AI access with interaction training and structured workflows will capture benefits more consistently than firms treating AI primarily as automation or cost reduction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a randomized student self-study experiment, with exam performance used as a proxy for knowledge-work productivity; broader organizational claims are interpretations and recommendations.
pts.d: The working paper reports recruitment of 179 Texas A&M students, mostly engineering undergraduates. Participants were randomized to non-LLM resources or free ChatGPT, with novice LLM users further randomized to standard use, conceptual scaffolding, additional study time, or peer collaboration. Average post-intervention scores were .56 (SD .26) with LLMs versus .48 (SD .23) without; the adjusted treatment effect was reported as p < .05. GPA and baseline-score interactions were nonsignificant (p = .59 and p = .2), while Treatment × AIC and a three-way interaction involving baseline knowledge were reported as p < .05. Scaffolded novices scored .45 (SD .14), compared with .38 (SD .22) for unguided novices; both the mean difference and scaffolding-by-AIC interaction were reported at .05 < p < .10. Additional-time novices scored .37, with no significant advantage. There were 20 withdrawals in the baseline group and nine in the LLM group; the authors interpret this imbalance as evidence of motivation and resource preference. Analyses use completers, and the paper acknowledges attrition bias. The discussion reports approximately 47% higher novice standard deviation with unguided AI and nearly 40% lower dispersion with scaffolding. It also asserts that 60–90-minute micro-training and workflow routines can raise the performance floor and reduce variance, but the described randomized arms do not include a separate micro-training intervention. AIC's operational measurement is not consistently described: the survey lists self-assessed AIC, while the results say AIC was behaviorally inferred and not self-assessed. These reporting distinctions preserve the evidence basis without treating the organizational extrapolations as separately measured workplace outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Measured effects concern a three-day learning intervention; the source offers present-oriented organizational implications without a dated long-term forecast.
pts.d: The source is identified as a 2026 working paper. Participants studied LLMs for three consecutive days, normally at least three hours daily; the additional-time arm required four hours daily. The AI condition restricted participants to free ChatGPT, with paid subscriptions prohibited. Post-study assessment occurred at the end of this period, and participants could bring a one-page cheat sheet. Thus, the measured outcome is short-term technical learning under study instructions and performance incentives, rather than sustained workplace output. The authors condition gains on users' AIC and on workflow support. They qualify their separate discussion of baseline knowledge and learning-gain patterns as exploratory, noting that the main treatment-by-baseline-score interaction is nonsignificant. Their organizational claims concern analogous activities such as analysis, synthesis, writing, and decision support; no long-term follow-up, employment forecast, or timetable for professional transformation is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is university learners; the authors extend their implications to early-career knowledge workers and organizations managing AI adoption.
pts.d: Among participants, high-AIC users capture disproportionate benefits, and low-AIC novices are identified as particularly needing conceptual guidance. Traditional academic markers are said not to distinguish treatment gains reliably. Enthusiastic but less competent users may prefer AI without using it effectively, while competent but reluctant users may favor social learning. Beyond the experiment, the authors identify knowledge-intensive organizations—including consulting, finance, analytics, design, engineering, research, and professional services—as affected by uneven AI capability. Managers and workforce-development teams are urged to diagnose AIC gaps, teach prompting and human verification of outputs, and provide templates, checklists, and feedback. These are claims about human–AI augmentation and organizational consistency, not evidence of lawyer replacement, legal-market restructuring, or access-to-justice outcomes.
